blocks.en: Introduction: The Shoemaker Who Reopened the Commission
blocks.es_reference: Introducción: El Zapatero Que Reabrió la Comisión

blocks.en: For nearly two centuries after the Reformation, the Protestant churches sent almost no foreign missionaries. Then, at the close of the eighteenth century, God raised up an obscure English shoemaker who would reopen the Great Commission for the whole church and set in motion what historians call the modern missionary movement — the greatest era of gospel expansion the world had ever seen. His name was William Carey, and he is rightly remembered as the father of modern missions.
blocks.es_reference: Por casi dos siglos después de la Reforma, las iglesias protestantes no enviaron casi ningún misionero al extranjero. Entonces, al final del siglo dieciocho, Dios levantó a un humilde zapatero inglés que reabriría la Gran Comisión para toda la iglesia y pondría en marcha lo que los historiadores llaman el movimiento misionero moderno — la mayor era de expansión del evangelio que el mundo había visto jamás. Su nombre era William Carey, y con razón se le recuerda como el padre de las misiones modernas.

blocks.en: I. The Shoemaker with a Map on His Wall
blocks.es_reference: I. El Zapatero con un Mapa en la Pared

blocks.en: William Carey (1761–1834) was a poor shoemaker from the English county of Northamptonshire. He had little formal schooling, yet he was a born student: largely self-taught, by his early twenties he could read the New Testament in Greek, Latin, Hebrew, French, and Dutch. As he sat mending shoes at his bench, he kept a homemade map of the world pinned to the wall, with notes on the peoples and lands he had read about. And as he worked, he wept over the millions in those lands who had never once heard the name of Christ. God had placed a burden for the whole world on the heart of a village tradesman.
blocks.es_reference: William Carey (1761–1834) era un pobre zapatero del condado inglés de Northamptonshire. Tuvo poca educación formal, pero era un estudiante nato: en gran parte autodidacta, para principios de sus veinte años podía leer el Nuevo Testamento en griego, latín, hebreo, francés y holandés. Mientras remendaba zapatos en su banco, mantenía un mapa del mundo hecho a mano clavado en la pared, con notas sobre los pueblos y las tierras de las que había leído. Y mientras trabajaba, lloraba por los millones en aquellas tierras que nunca habían oído ni una vez el nombre de Cristo. Dios había puesto una carga por el mundo entero en el corazón de un artesano de aldea.

blocks.en: II. The Argument He Had to Answer
blocks.es_reference: II. El Argumento Que Tuvo Que Responder

blocks.en: The Baptists of Carey's day were strong on doctrine but weak on missionary obligation. The view that dominated their thinking held that the Great Commission had been given to the apostles only, and that if God intended to save the heathen, He would do it in His own way, without the help of human means. According to the well-known account, when the young Carey dared to raise the question of missions among his fellow ministers, an older man told him, "Sit down, young man; when God is pleased to convert the heathen, He will do it without your aid or mine." This is the hyper-Calvinist error — the mistake of confusing the sovereignty of God with the idleness of man.
blocks.es_reference: Los bautistas de los días de Carey eran fuertes en doctrina pero débiles en obligación misionera. La opinión que dominaba su pensamiento sostenía que la Gran Comisión había sido dada solo a los apóstoles, y que si Dios se proponía salvar a los paganos, lo haría a su propia manera, sin la ayuda de medios humanos. Según el conocido relato, cuando el joven Carey se atrevió a plantear la cuestión de las misiones entre sus colegas ministros, un hombre mayor le dijo: "Siéntese, joven; cuando Dios se digne convertir a los paganos, lo hará sin la ayuda de usted ni la mía." Este es el error hipercalvinista — la equivocación de confundir la soberanía de Dios con la ociosidad del hombre.

blocks.en: III. The Enquiry
blocks.es_reference: III. La Investigación

blocks.en: In 1792 Carey answered that argument in print. His great pamphlet bore a long and pointed title: An Enquiry into the Obligations of Christians to Use Means for the Conversion of the Heathens. The very title carried the argument — Christians are under obligation to use means. From Scripture, from history, and from the geography of his own day, Carey showed that the Great Commission still bound every Christian, and that God ordinarily works through means: through messengers who are sent, supported, and sustained. It stands among the most important documents in the whole history of missions.
blocks.es_reference: En 1792 Carey respondió a aquel argumento por escrito. Su gran folleto llevaba un título largo y certero: Una Investigación sobre las Obligaciones de los Cristianos de Usar Medios para la Conversión de los Paganos. El título mismo encerraba el argumento — los cristianos están bajo la obligación de usar medios. Desde la Escritura, desde la historia, y desde la geografía de su propio día, Carey mostró que la Gran Comisión todavía obligaba a todo cristiano, y que Dios ordinariamente obra por medios: por medio de mensajeros que son enviados, sostenidos y sustentados. Está entre los documentos más importantes de toda la historia de las misiones.

blocks.en: IV. Expect Great Things; Attempt Great Things
blocks.es_reference: IV. Esperar Grandes Cosas; Intentar Grandes Cosas

blocks.en: In May of 1792 Carey preached a sermon at Nottingham on the words of Isaiah 54: "Enlarge the place of your tent... for you shall expand to the right and to the left, and your descendants will inherit the nations" (Isaiah 54:2–3, NKJV). From that sermon came the words that would become the motto of the modern missionary movement: "Expect great things from God; attempt great things for God." Carey's brethren were stirred, and within months a small band of them founded the Baptist Missionary Society to send him out — the first of the great mission societies that would carry the gospel around the world.
blocks.es_reference: En mayo de 1792 Carey predicó un sermón en Nottingham sobre las palabras de Isaías 54: "Ensancha el sitio de tu tienda... porque a la mano derecha y a la mano izquierda te extenderás; y tu simiente heredará a las naciones" (Isaías 54:2–3, RVG). De aquel sermón salieron las palabras que llegarían a ser el lema del movimiento misionero moderno: "Esperad grandes cosas de Dios; intentad grandes cosas para Dios." Los hermanos de Carey fueron conmovidos, y en cuestión de meses un pequeño grupo de ellos fundó la Sociedad Misionera Bautista para enviarlo — la primera de las grandes sociedades misioneras que llevarían el evangelio alrededor del mundo.

blocks.en: V. Forty-One Years in India
blocks.es_reference: V. Cuarenta y Un Años en la India

blocks.en: In 1793 Carey sailed for India, and he never saw England again. He labored there for forty-one years without a single furlough home. With his colleagues Joshua Marshman and William Ward — the famous "Serampore Trio" — he translated the Bible, in whole or in part, into more than thirty Indian languages. He founded Serampore College in 1818, the first Christian institution of higher learning in Asia. He waited seven long years for his first Indian convert, buried a child and saw his wife's health break on the field, and still he would not quit. The shoemaker had become the father of modern missions.
blocks.es_reference: En 1793 Carey zarpó hacia la India, y nunca volvió a ver Inglaterra. Trabajó allí cuarenta y un años sin un solo permiso para volver a casa. Con sus colegas Joshua Marshman y William Ward — el famoso "Trío de Serampore" — tradujo la Biblia, entera o en parte, a más de treinta idiomas de la India. Fundó el Colegio de Serampore en 1818, la primera institución cristiana de educación superior en Asia. Esperó siete largos años por su primer converso indio, sepultó a un hijo y vio quebrantarse la salud de su esposa en el campo, y aun así no quiso rendirse. El zapatero se había convertido en el padre de las misiones modernas.

blocks.en: VI. The Century He Opened
blocks.es_reference: VI. El Siglo Que Abrió

blocks.en: Carey did not labor alone for long. The movement he set in motion swept across the next hundred years, until the nineteenth century became the greatest single century of Christian expansion since Pentecost. In the year 1800, perhaps one in a hundred of the world's Christians lived outside Europe and North America; by 1900 the gospel had reached every continent, planted churches in hundreds of languages, and raised up native believers on every shore. One obedient shoemaker, who simply refused to believe that the Great Commission had expired, opened the door for them all.
blocks.es_reference: Carey no trabajó solo por mucho tiempo. El movimiento que puso en marcha barrió los siguientes cien años, hasta que el siglo diecinueve se convirtió en el mayor siglo individual de expansión cristiana desde Pentecostés. En el año 1800, quizás uno de cada cien de los cristianos del mundo vivía fuera de Europa y Norteamérica; para 1900 el evangelio había llegado a cada continente, plantado iglesias en cientos de idiomas, y levantado creyentes nativos en cada costa. Un zapatero obediente, que sencillamente se negó a creer que la Gran Comisión había expirado, abrió la puerta para todos ellos.

blocks.en: Conclusion: Great Things from a Great God
blocks.es_reference: Conclusión: Grandes Cosas de un Gran Dios

blocks.en: Carey teaches us that God delights to use the obscure and the ordinary. He had no wealth, no fame, and no earthly advantage — only a burden for the lost, a settled confidence in the promises of God, and the courage to act upon them. "Expect great things from God; attempt great things for God." The same God who sent a village shoemaker to India is the God who calls and sends today, and He is still looking for ordinary men and women who will attempt great things in His name.
blocks.es_reference: Carey nos enseña que Dios se deleita en usar a los oscuros y a los ordinarios. No tenía riqueza, ni fama, ni ventaja terrenal alguna — solo una carga por los perdidos, una confianza firme en las promesas de Dios, y el valor de actuar sobre ellas. "Esperad grandes cosas de Dios; intentad grandes cosas para Dios." El mismo Dios que envió a un zapatero de aldea a la India es el Dios que llama y envía hoy, y todavía está buscando a hombres y mujeres ordinarios que intenten grandes cosas en su nombre.

sa.prompt: Who was William Carey, and why is he called the father of modern missions?
sa.model: William Carey (1761-1834) was a poor, largely self-taught English shoemaker who became the father of modern missions because he reopened the Great Commission for the whole church after nearly two centuries of Protestant neglect of foreign missions. He answered the dominant apostles-only view of his day, sailed for India in 1793, and set in motion the modern missionary movement that transformed the nineteenth century into the greatest era of gospel expansion since Pentecost.

sa.prompt: Describe Carey before his missionary work — his trade, his learning, and the map on his wall.
sa.model: Before his missionary work, Carey was a poor shoemaker from Northamptonshire with little formal schooling, yet largely self-taught he could read the New Testament in Greek, Latin, Hebrew, French, and Dutch by his early twenties. As he mended shoes at his bench, he kept a homemade map of the world pinned to the wall with notes on unreached peoples, and he wept over the millions who had never heard the name of Christ.

sa.prompt: What was the dominant view Carey had to answer, and why does the lesson call it an error?
sa.model: The dominant view Carey had to answer held that the Great Commission had been given to the apostles only, and that if God intended to save the heathen, He would do it without human means — an older minister famously told Carey to 'sit down' since God would convert the heathen without his aid. The lesson calls this a hyper-Calvinist error because it confuses the sovereignty of God with the idleness of man, wrongly assuming that trusting God's sovereignty means we need not act.

sa.prompt: Explain Carey's pamphlet, the Enquiry, and what it argued.
sa.model: Carey's pamphlet, An Enquiry into the Obligations of Christians to Use Means for the Conversion of the Heathens (1792), argued from Scripture, history, and geography that Christians are under obligation to use means — that the Great Commission still bound every believer, and that God ordinarily works through messengers who are sent, supported, and sustained rather than by bypassing human effort entirely.

sa.prompt: What was Carey's famous motto, and what sermon and text gave rise to it?
sa.model: Carey's famous motto was 'Expect great things from God; attempt great things for God.' It arose from a sermon he preached at Nottingham in May 1792 on Isaiah 54:2-3, which speaks of enlarging the place of one's tent because one's descendants will inherit the nations — the sermon stirred his brethren and led within months to the founding of the Baptist Missionary Society.

sa.prompt: Describe Carey's forty-one years in India, including the Serampore Trio and the translation work.
sa.model: Carey sailed for India in 1793 and never saw England again, laboring there for forty-one years without a single furlough home. With colleagues Joshua Marshman and William Ward, known as the Serampore Trio, he translated the Bible, in whole or in part, into more than thirty Indian languages, and founded Serampore College in 1818, the first Christian institution of higher learning in Asia, despite waiting seven years for his first Indian convert and burying a child on the field.

sa.prompt: What does the founding of the Baptist Missionary Society show about how missionaries are sent?
sa.model: The founding of the Baptist Missionary Society shows that missionaries are not meant to send themselves — Carey's stirred brethren organized to formally send and support him, becoming the first of the great mission societies that would carry the gospel around the world. It demonstrates the pattern of organized, corporate sending rather than isolated individual initiative.

sa.prompt: Why does the lesson call the nineteenth century the greatest century of Christian expansion since Pentecost?
sa.model: The lesson calls the nineteenth century the greatest single century of Christian expansion since Pentecost because in the year 1800 perhaps only one in a hundred of the world's Christians lived outside Europe and North America, but by 1900 the gospel had reached every continent, planted churches in hundreds of languages, and raised up native believers on every shore — an unprecedented explosion of gospel expansion in a single century.

sa.prompt: What does Carey's life teach about whom God uses for missions?
sa.model: Carey's life teaches that God delights to use the obscure and the ordinary — he had no wealth, no fame, and no earthly advantage, only a burden for the lost and a settled confidence in God's promises. His story shows that great impact for the kingdom does not require impressive credentials, only a willing, obedient heart.

sa.prompt: Carey said, 'Expect great things from God; attempt great things for God.' What great thing might God be calling you to expect and attempt?
sa.model: This is a personal reflection question inviting the student to consider what great thing God might be calling them to expect and attempt, following Carey's example of bold faith paired with concrete action. A thoughtful answer names a specific area — whether in missions, ministry, or another calling — where the student senses God inviting them to trust Him for more than seems humanly possible.
